facts.fact_text: The applicants are members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden – PIRIN ("UMO Ilinden – PIRIN").
On 3 August 1998, the second applicant, acting on behalf of the members and followers of UMO Ilinden – PIRIN, informed the mayor of Sofia that a rally had been planned for 10 August 1998.
On 1 September 1998, the first applicant, acting on behalf of the members and followers of UMO Ilinden – PIRIN, informed the mayor of Sofia that a rally had been planned for 12 September 1998.
Article 43(1) of the Constitution of Bulgaria of 1991 provides that everyone shall have the right to peaceful and unarmed assembly at meetings and marches.
On 3 August 1998, the mayor of Sofia issued an order prohibiting the rally planned for 10 August 1998.
On 2 September 1998, the mayor of Sofia issued an order banning the rally planned for 12 September 1998.
Since on 12 September 1998 the mayor of Sofia's ban on the rally had not been overturned, the applicants informed the members and followers of UMO Ilinden – PIRIN that the rally would not take place.
The mayor of Sofia's order prohibiting the rally planned for 10 August 1998 was issued pursuant to section 12(2)(2) of the Meetings and Marches Act.
The mayor of Sofia's order banning the rally planned for 12 September 1998 was issued pursuant to section 12(2)(2) of the Meetings and Marches Act.
The legal requirements for the organisation of meetings are laid down in the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 ("Закон за събранията, митингите и манифестациите").
The mayor of Sofia opined, without giving further reasons, that the rally planned for 10 August 1998 would "create conditions for breaches of the public order".
The mayor of Sofia's order banning the rally planned for 12 September 1998 stated that the event would "create conditions for breaches of the public order", without giving further reasons.
The mayor of Sofia opined, without giving further reasons, that the rally planned for 10 August 1998 would "create conditions for breaches of the public order".
The mayor of Sofia's order banning the rally planned for 12 September 1998 stated that the event would "create conditions for breaches of the public order", without giving further reasons.
The first applicant argued before the Sofia District Court that the mayor of Sofia's order banning the rally planned for 12 September 1998 was not reasoned.
The first applicant argued before the Sofia District Court that there were no grounds to anticipate that the rally planned for 12 September 1998 would pose a threat to public order.

The first applicant argued before the Sofia District Court that allowing local authorities to prohibit public events without specifying reasons would render nugatory the legal guarantees of freedom of assembly.

On 8 September 1998, the Sofia District Court ruled in private that it had no jurisdiction to examine the first applicant's appeal against the mayor of Sofia's order banning the rally planned for 12 September 1998.

The Sofia District Court held that the mayor of Sofia's order banning the rally planned for 12 September 1998 had to be appealed first before the Executive Committee of the People's Council, as provided in section 12(4) of the Meetings and Marches Act.
The Sofia District Court held that the person concerned could resort to the court only if an appeal to the Executive Committee of the People's Council was unsuccessful.
The Sofia District Court discontinued the judicial proceedings concerning the first applicant's appeal and sent the appeal to the Executive Committee of the People's Council.
The Sofia District Court's ruling of 8 September 1998 was apparently not notified to the first applicant.
The first applicant argued before the Sofia City Court that the Sofia District Court had erred in referring the appeal to the Executive Committee of the People's Council.

The first applicant argued that the Executive Committee of the People's Council was mentioned in the Meetings and Marches Act, which had been enacted prior to the Constitution of 1991, when the municipal authorities had been structured differently.

The first applicant argued that under the Constitution of 1991, the Executive Committee of the People's Council, which had been part of the executive branch of the local authorities, had ceased to exist.

The first applicant argued that it was erroneous to hold that the Municipal Council – the municipal legislative body – was the successor to the Executive Committee of the People's Council and as such competent to examine appeals against orders of the mayor.
The first applicant argued that the Municipal Council convened at long intervals, which had prevented it from examining the appeal in time for the rally planned for 12 September 1998.
On 19 March 2002, the Sofia City Court dismissed the first applicant's appeal against the Sofia District Court's ruling of 8 September 1998.

The Sofia City Court held that by section 12(4) of the Meetings and Marches Act, the organiser of a rally could appeal against the mayoral ban to the Municipal Council, which had to rule on the appeal within twenty-four hours.
The Sofia City Court held that only if the Municipal Council dismissed the appeal could the dispute be brought before the court.

The Sofia City Court held that by section 35(2) of the Administrative Procedure Act, judicial review of administrative acts was only possible if the administrative remedies had been exhausted or the time-limit for doing so had expired.

The Sofia City Court held that in the case at hand no administrative appeal had been lodged, whereas the appeal to the Sofia District Court had been lodged on 2 September 1998, i.e. before the expiry of the twenty-four hours' time-limit laid down in section 12(4) of the Meetings and Marches Act.

The Sofia City Court held that the argument that the Municipal Council convened at long intervals and was hence not in a position to examine the appeal in time was unavailing, because an infelicitous legal rule still had to be complied with.

The Sofia City Court held that if the administrative body failed to rule on the appeal within twenty-four hours, the planned event could take place, as provided by section 12(5) of the Meetings and Marches Act.

The Sofia City Court held that the Municipal Council had the power to rule on an appeal against the mayoral ban, because by the terms of section 21(2) of the Local Self-Government and Local Administration Act it could decide on all questions of importance for the local community.
The first applicant appealed to the Supreme Court of Cassation against the Sofia City Court's decision of 19 March 2002, reiterating his arguments.
On 11 March 2003, the Supreme Court of Cassation dismissed the first applicant's appeal in a final decision.
The Supreme Court of Cassation held that the Sofia City Court's disposition of the case had been correct, although it did not support the reasoning given by the Sofia City Court.

The Supreme Court of Cassation held that by the time the Sofia City Court had decided the case – more than three and a half years after the date of the rally planned for 12 September 1998 – the first applicant had no longer had any interest in appealing against the ban.

The Supreme Court of Cassation held that the first applicant's interest in appealing against the ban had been lacking even at the time of the lodging of the appeal against the Sofia District Court's ruling.

Section 12(2) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the President of the Executive Committee of the People's Council or the mayor shall be competent to prohibit the holding of a meeting, rally or march where reliable information exists that: (1) it aims at the violent overturning of Constitutional public order or is directed against the territorial integrity of the country; (2) it would endanger public order in the local community; or (4) it would breach the rights and freedoms of others.

Section 12(4) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the organiser of the meeting, rally or march may appeal to the Executive Committee of the People's Council against the prohibition, and the Executive Committee shall decide within twenty-four hours.

Section 12(5) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that where the Executive Committee of the People's Council has not decided within the twenty-four hour time-limit, the march, rally or meeting may proceed.

Section 12(6) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that if the appeal is dismissed, the dispute shall be referred to the respective district court which shall decide within five days, and that court's decision shall be final.
The Meetings and Marches Act was enacted in 1990, when the Constitution of 1971 was still in force.
Under the Constitution of 1971, the executive local state organs were the Executive Committees of the district People's Councils.

Under the Constitution of 1971, the mayors referred to in some provisions of the Meetings and Marches Act were representatives of the Executive Committee acting in villages and towns under the jurisdiction of the respective People's Council.
The Constitution of Bulgaria of 1991 abolished the Executive Committees of the People's Councils.
The Constitution of Bulgaria of 1991 established the post of mayor, elected by direct universal suffrage, as the "organ of the executive power in the municipality" under Article 139(1).

The general rules of procedure for administrative appeals and judicial review of administrative acts are set out in the Administrative Procedure Act of 1979 ("Закон за административното производство").
Section 19(1) of the Administrative Procedure Act of 1979 provides that administrative acts may be appealed hierarchically before the higher administrative body or official.

Section 27(1) of the Administrative Procedure Act of 1979 provides that the appeal must be examined by the administrative body or official which is immediately superior to the body or official which issued the act.
Section 27(3) of the Administrative Procedure Act of 1979 provides that the acts of the mayors may be appealed before the regional governors.
Section 33(1) of the Administrative Procedure Act of 1979 provides that administrative acts may also be appealed before the competent courts.

Section 35(2) of the Administrative Procedure Act of 1979 provides that the appeal to the courts must be lodged after the administrative remedies have been exhausted or the time-limit for doing so has expired.
Section 21(1) of the Local Self-Government and Local Administration Act of 1991 ("Закон за местното самоуправление и местната администрация") contains a list of the powers of the Municipal Council.
Section 21(1) of the Local Self-Government and Local Administration Act of 1991 makes no mention of a power of the Municipal Council to examine appeals against acts of the mayor.

Section 21(2) of the Local Self-Government and Local Administration Act of 1991 provides that the Municipal Council is generally competent to decide on matters of importance for the local community which do not fall within the competence of other bodies.
